w: Began in 1879 as a lumber baron's private gallery; Thomas Barlow Walker's collection became the Walker Art Gallery in 1927, then the Walker Art Center in 1940 with WPA support. Herzog & de Meuron's 2005 addition wrapped the 1971 Edward Larrabee Barnes building; its sculpture garden helps draw 700,000 visitors yearly.
s: A lumber baron's gallery, grown into a modern art hub
_facts: Founded 1879 as Thomas Barlow Walker's private gallery
Became Walker Art Center in 1940 with WPA support
1971 building by Edward Larrabee Barnes, expanded 2005 by Herzog & de Meuron
Around 700,000 annual visitors with the adjacent Sculpture Garden

w: Built on bluffs above where the Minnesota meets the Mississippi, finished in 1825 as Fort Snelling. Officers here kept enslaved people, including Dred and Harriet Scott, whose years at the fort fed his Supreme Court freedom suit. In 1862 it held Dakota and Ho-Chunk families before their forced removal from Minnesota.
s: The fort that shaped Dred Scott's case and Dakota exile
_facts: Completed 1825 at the confluence of the Minnesota and Mississippi Rivers
Dred and Harriet Scott lived here as enslaved people in the 1830s
Site of a concentration camp for Dakota and Ho-Chunk people after the 1862 war
Decommissioned 1946, lower post restored from 1965

w: Minneapolis's largest lake now carries its Dakota name, Bde Maka Ska, after decades known as Lake Calhoun. Part of the city's Chain of Lakes, it covers 401 acres and reaches 87 feet deep, ringed by park land and a path loop that makes it one of the city's busiest outdoor gathering spots.
s: The city's largest lake, restored to its Dakota name
_facts: 401 acres, maximum depth 87 feet
Formerly known as Lake Calhoun, renamed Bde Maka Ska
Part of Minneapolis's Chain of Lakes
Ringed by park land and bike/walking trails

w: Dedicated in 1913 on Hennepin Avenue, this Catholic church became the first basilica in the United States when Pope Pius XI elevated it in 1926. It now serves as co-cathedral for the Archdiocese of Saint Paul and Minneapolis, a status it shares with the cathedral across the river.
s: America's first basilica, elevated by Rome in 1926
_facts: Dedicated 1913 on Hennepin Avenue
First basilica designated in the United States, in 1926
Co-cathedral of the Archdiocese of Saint Paul and Minneapolis

w: Long and Kees's 1888 municipal fortress doubles as Hennepin County Courthouse, its granite mass jointly run by a city-county commission that still splits occupancy 60-40. Locals note its close resemblance to the city halls of Cincinnati and Toronto, products of the same late-Victorian civic-monument era.
s: A joint city-county fortress echoing Cincinnati's city hall
_facts: Built 1888, designed by Long and Kees
Jointly owned and run by the city and Hennepin County
On the National Register of Historic Places since 1974
Resembles the city halls of Cincinnati and Toronto

w: Founded in 1963 after Tyrone Guthrie, disenchanted with Broadway, set out to build a resident repertory company for classic plays. Its original Ralph Rapson building held a 1,441-seat thrust stage until 2006; the company then moved into its current Jean Nouvel-designed home by the Mississippi.
_facts: Founded 1963 by Tyrone Guthrie, Oliver Rea and Peter Zeisler
Original 1963-2006 building had a 1,441-seat thrust stage designed by Tanya Moiseiwitsch
Moved in 2006 to a building designed by Jean Nouvel
Won the Regional Theatre Tony Award in 1982

w: Built inside the ruins of the 1870s Washburn 'A' Mill on the Mississippi's bank, this Minnesota Historical Society museum opened in 2003 next to Mill Ruins Park. It traces how hydropower from Saint Anthony Falls made Minneapolis the flour-milling capital of America, using the ruined mill itself as the exhibit hall.
s: A flour-milling museum built inside a mill's own ruins
_facts: Housed in the ruined 1870s Washburn 'A' Mill
Opened 2003, run by the Minnesota Historical Society
Sits within the St. Anthony Falls Historic District
Tells the story of Minneapolis flour milling via Saint Anthony Falls hydropower

w: One of six islands that once dotted Saint Anthony Falls, Nicollet Island survived only because engineers halted the falls' northward creep in the late 1800s; its neighbors were destroyed or fused to the bank. It carried the first bridge ever built across the Mississippi, opened in 1855.
s: The one falls-side island that outlasted its neighbors
_facts: One of six islands once near Saint Anthony Falls; the rest vanished or merged with the bank
Site of the first bridge across the Mississippi River, opened 1855
2000 census population of 144
Named for cartographer Joseph Nicollet

w: Opened in 1956 as the first fully enclosed, climate-controlled shopping mall in America, Southdale was architect Victor Gruen's attempt to build an indoor town square as a counter to car-centric sprawl. It has weathered vacancies and renovations since, but much of Gruen's original structure survives.
s: America's first enclosed mall, built to fight sprawl
_facts: Opened 1956 in Edina, a Twin Cities suburb
First fully enclosed, climate-controlled shopping mall in the US
Designed by Victor Gruen as an anti-car-centric urban space
About 1.3 million sq ft of leasable space with 106 retail tenants

w: Bill and Sidney Volk built this single-screen cinema in 1948, then returned to give its lobby an ultramodern overhaul in 1956. One of the last surviving single-screen theaters in the Twin Cities, it stuck to second-run films until COVID pushed it toward first-run releases.
s: A 1948 single-screen cinema still running strong
_facts: Built 1948 by Bill and Sidney Volk, designed by Liebenberg and Kaplan
Lobby renovated in an ultramodern style in 1956
One of the few surviving single-screen cinemas in the Twin Cities
Switched from second-run to first-run films during the COVID-19 pandemic

w: A speakeasy from 1928, the 5-8 Club is one of two Minneapolis bars claiming to have invented the Juicy Lucy, a cheeseburger stuffed with molten cheese, in the 1950s - a rivalry it still runs with Matt's Bar. It has since added three more Minnesota locations, but stays known for the original.
s: A speakeasy that claims to have invented the Juicy Lucy
_facts: Founded 1928 as a speakeasy
Claims, alongside rival Matt's Bar, to have invented the Juicy Lucy burger in the 1950s
Also serves a Saucy Sally burger and fried cheese curds
Now has three additional Minnesota locations

w: This deck-arch span carries State Highways 55 and 62 over the Minnesota River just before it meets the Mississippi at 'Mendota,' Dakota for the meeting of the waters. From the bridge, both the Minneapolis and Saint Paul skylines are visible at once, a rare double view over the point where the two rivers merge.
s: Where two rivers meet, and both skylines appear at once
_facts: Carries State Highways 55 and 62 over the Minnesota River
Final bridge over the Minnesota River before it joins the Mississippi
'Mendota' is Dakota for the meeting of the waters
Both Minneapolis and Saint Paul skylines visible from the bridge

w: Founded in 1878, Temple Israel is Minneapolis's oldest synagogue and remains one of the largest Reform Jewish congregations anywhere in the country, still anchoring the city's Jewish community from its longstanding home.
_facts: Founded 1878
Oldest synagogue in Minneapolis
One of the largest Reform Jewish congregations in the United States
